items.body:
Ocean Cage is a live recording of Tianzhuo Chen and Siko Setyanto’s performance Moyang & Seaman – a stage work that evolved from the immersive theatre performance project Ocean Cage, sharing the same title.

"Directed by Tianzhuo Chen, aka Asiandopeboys, the immersive performance Ocean Cage merges scenography, installation, choreography, and live music into a unified whole. Inspired by the complex whaling traditions in Lamalera, an Indonesian village that preservers ritualised whaling practices and ancestral beliefs, the work unfolds through interconnected trinities – Moyang (ancestor), Lera Wulan (god), and Seaman – all incarnated by Siko Setyanto. It tells a porous story of unlocking the cage of the ocean: receiving ancestral blessing while becoming entangled with misjudgement, misunderstanding, ecological grief, and temporal displacement, until the sacrifice and life cycles move toward equilibrium.

Evolving from this larger narration, Moyang 先祖 & Seaman 漁 師 shifts into a frontal, meditative dialogues between ancestor and seaman. Inspired by Japanese Noh theatre and deeply rooted in Nusantara traditions, the performance integrates music, dance, and stage art into a mutable and fluid process, continuing to explore ancestral presences, cyclical time, and spiritual transformation.

The album features music by KADAPAT and Nova Ruth, interwoven with Siko Setyanto’s narrations and monologues. KADAPAT’s electronic-gamelan practice moves through interlocking rhythm and cyclical time structures, extending asymmetrical Balinese ancestral yet modern sonic with digital signal. Bamboo and metal, folk and sacred, horizontal and vertical forces collide and co-exist, forming layered pulses that shift and reform in motion.

As Siko beautifully summarises the creative synergy in Ocean Cage/Moyang & Seaman: “Being on stage is like sailing together into the unknown – embracing every mystery that comes our way.” The album of Ocean Cage also records the reciprocal, communal, improvisational, polymetric, and relational collaborations among Nova Ruth, Siko Setyanto, KADAPAT and Tianzhuo Chen. No role is fixed; no expression remains confined to its original context. In this sense, Ocean Cage becomes an assembled living being."

items.body:
‘ИМА (Ima)’ is a work by KiMiMi, the solo project of a musician Shin-ya Ohno, which captures the layers of time and the presence of people inhabiting ‘Arimasuton Building’―a self-built structure created over 20 years by architect Keisuke Oka, located in Mita, Tokyo, and reconstructs them into music.

"A multi-instrumentalist who masterfully handles a diverse range of instruments, with the gaida (an ancestor of the bagpipes) – which he studied in Bulgaria – at the core of his sound, KiMiMi has previously brought traces of daily life and folk melodies recorded during his travels back to the scale of home recording, weaving fantastical folk soundscapes through cassette tape works and stage music.

Alongside his musical activities, he has participated in the construction work for ‘Arimasuton Building’, recording the sounds of hammers and steel beams echoing on site, lunchtime chatter, the melodies of instruments played by others, and the sound of cars passing by. From the end of 2022, a zine titled ‘Monthly Arimasuton Building Urimasu’, based on this construction project, was launched. KiMiMi incorporates these recordings into the musical works he contributes to each issue, layering sounds from live instruments―including the gaida, accordion, guitar, flute, ukulele, piano, foot-pump organ, melodica and xylophone―alongside a few synthesiser tones, to shape a soundscape imbued with the humidity and breath of the site.

KiMiMi’s creative process is characterised not by planned construction, but by an attitude of entrusting the work to chance, intuition and the passage of time. Fragmented recordings are layered, set aside for a time, and then unearthed again. Through this repetition, the music naturally takes shape. This resonates perfectly with the process of ‘Arimasuton Building’, which was built up improvisationally, layer by layer, without any pre-prepared blueprints.

‘ИМА (Ima)’ marks the current stage of KiMiMi’s sonic journey and represents an attempt to gracefully transcend the boundaries between architecture and music, documentation and creation, and the individual and the community. The clamour of the city, the tranquillity of manual labour, laughter, and every sound resonating at the Arimasuton Building site blend with KiMiMi’s music, reflecting the very passage of time in which people live."

items.body:
Smacking that sweetspot between grime, techno, bassline and soca, Anthoney J Hart (East Man, Imaginary Forces) aka Basic Rhythm delivers a full-bore pack of rampers for Bristol-via-Berlin’s bassbin overlords, Sneaker Social Club.

Active in a vein of uchronic, ‘nuum-bending invention since the 2010’s, but with roots reaching back to ‘90s pirate radio, Hart’s decade-straddling steez yields the crankiest horsepower as Basic Rhythm on ‘8 Bar Techno’. Hewing hard to the brief, he dissects and recombines styles & patterns with a fiercely upfront quality, trampling on putative borders with a rudeboy alacrity that works a treat on up-for -it ‘floors.

The durable torsion of OG jungle tekno and its myriad derivations are twisted into tensile girders, variously splitting the difference between 4/4 grime and hard groove techno in ‘the title tune, or panel-beating sublow into rictus bashiness on ‘Weed Killer’, while firing killer rounds of vocal cuts including the dancehall-grime of ‘Vibez’ with NyNy, or electroid drill with Lyrical Strally and Eklipse.

Along with the precision-tooled rufige of ‘Kонец века’ with Moscow Legend, the mutant soca gallop o ‘Ice cold’, and diesel-fuelled grime-techno of ‘More Pricks than Kicks’, or the dive-bombing darkness of ‘The Deluge’, it’s a hard set for discerning 140BPM shotters, and surely one of Basic Rhythm’s deadliest.

items.body:
Hanoi-based artist Trần Uy Đức, who's been spotted alongside Vietnamese avant-garde collective Rắn Cạp Đuôi, arrives on Lolina's Relaxin imprint with 'ByyShh', a set of warped pop experiments, casual electro abstractions and glitched-out sketches that'll make perfect sense if yr into Voice Actor, LA Timpa or even Tujiko Noriko.

There's no real sense of continuity to 'ByyShh', and that's why it's so refreshing. Đức has been releasing material since 2018, working as a video artist and a designer as well as putting together wonky deployments like 2021's noise-caked 'Came' and 2024's curiously poppy 'It Whims'. 'ByyShh' is his most high profile release yet and straddles the length and breadth of his output, bounding from idea to idea with a relentless level of engagement. Specific songs aren't overworked, they're dubbed sketchily - for posterity, more than anything - before Đức moves onto the next. Opener 'Dessert', for example, is a jerky set of guitar riffs and ring modulated belches that Đức arranges into a jaunty march, while 'Play With Me (Deep Down It’s So Hard)' is sci-fi R&B that sounds as if Timbaland was making a DIY melt movie soundtrack in 1982.

From moment to moment, Đức sounds as if he's flushing out his brain of ideas that have been marinating for decades. The surprisingly catchy 'Do It' lands somewhere between Enya's 'Orinoco Flow' and Daniel Johnson if someone had gifted him a voice modulator, and upfront single 'Like a Star' is a dembow banger attacked by an electric razor and a tape speed dial, slowing up and speeding up seemingly randomly while an incessant buzz takes the place of a lead synth. It's relentlessly outlandish, erratic material - perfectly at home on Relaxin, then.

items.body:
Originally released in 2016, German "dark folk" duo Brannten Schnüre's third album is even more atmospheric than its predecessors, a vision of the Bavarian winter that follows the St. Martin's Day procession - something like Bonfire Night muddled with Halloween, basically.

If you'd only heard 'Sommer Im Pfirsichhain' and 'Aprilnacht', the first two parts of Christian Schoppik and Katie Rich's seasonal quadrilogy, 'Geträumt hab ich vom Martinszug' (I dreamed about the St. Martin's Day procession) might come as a surprise. Here, Schoppik works into his samples and instrumental takes even more, sometimes leaving just faint traces of music in a sea of drones, glitches and ghost traces. It's like listening to sequence of inversions at first, with backmasked vocals and incomprehensible instrumentation: head over to the Caretaker-like 'Da Unten Leuchten Wir', or the noise-caked freeform lullaby 'Unser Zug Führt Durch Die Stadt'. If it's music that's supposed to represent a dream of St. Martin's Day, rather than the even itself, it makes perfect sense.

To an outsider, it's a strange event. There's a parade of children with homemade paper lanterns that usually begins at a local church and is sometimes led by a person dressed in Roman gear, then there's a bonfire and a festive meal that doesn't look that different from a Thanksgiving spread. Schoppik and Rich's eccentric songs - like the organ-led 'Damit Die Zähne Wieder Glänzen' - are peppered between haunted, scene-setting hypnagogic moments, like the woozed 'Lösche Aus Dein Licht' or the genius 'Rote, Gelbe, Grüne, Blaue', five-and-a-half-minutes of downsampled gurgles, decelerated accordion gusts and distant footsteps. Properly good stuff - if you enjoyed Schoppik and Rich's 2022 Freundliche Kreisel album, or Schoppik's solo material as Läuten der Seele, this'll be essential listening.

items.body:
DAF legend & EBM pioneer Robert Görl tightens his bonds with OG Dorian Gray DJ, Sylvie Marks, on a sinuous debut duo LP referencing their illustrious history of Teutonic meat motors.

‘Dark Silver Moon Light’ binds the German club mavericks’ respective ideas on EBM, post-punk, industrial, and techno, thru 10 taut synth + sequencer workouts largely defined by motorik momentum and melancholic air which guides them to brooding arp hymns and side quests into slower kraut sleaze. Some six years in the works, it effectively picks up where Robert & Sylvie left off with their completion and release of DAF’s final album, ‘Nur Noch Einer’ (2021), following the passing of his bandmate Gabi Delgado (1958-2020), with Sylvie ideally helping to fill Gabi’s role as spiritual spur to her pal.

Sylvie’s sharp DJ and club instincts, honed since her days as the first and only female DJ at Frankfurt’s resoundingly influential Dorian Gray club since the ‘90s, surely help keep Robert’s iconic sequences and steel-tipped drums on course for bodies in motion. It’s all maybe not as fierce as early DAF, but is still athletically toned and smacks below the belt on the fanged aces ‘Falscher Ton’ and ‘Wir brechen aus’, but the best bits more clearly project an air of restless gloom. From the shark-eyed swagger of ‘So wie Du bist’, thru a classy mid-section spanning the tortured troubadour turn of ‘Don’t Stay at Home’, a razor-riding title tune, and standout of Gerald Donald-esque finesse on ‘Der Fluss’, to the kerb-crawl cruise of ‘Es int die zu spät’, DAF’s legacy is in safe hands here.

But look a little further back in her catalogue and things will fall into place; remember 'Angels Pharmacy' and Rememb
items.body:
R&B outsider Zsela joins forces with inc. no world's Daniel Aged and film composer Taul Katz on '4 Dreams', a billowing ambient-neoclassical hallucination that'll tickle fans of Mary Lattimore, Malibu, Nala Sinephro, Gigi Masin.

If you only know Zsela thanks to her dramatic 2024 debut album 'Big For You', the mostly beatless, fully reflective '4 Dreams' might come as a surprise. But look a little further back in her catalogue and things will fall into place; remember 'Angels Pharmacy' and Remembrance' from Actress's 'Karma & Desire'? That was Zsela on vocals, so she's got priors. '4 Dreams' started life as the soundtrack to 'Seven Heavenly Senses', an art exhibition from last year at Paris's Hôtel de la Marine, but has since taken on a life of its own. Zsela's breaths are stretched and sculpted into warm, washing biomechanical pads on the opening dream, left to weather tinny arpeggiated FM synths and muggy bass drones. So far, so predictable. But Zsela muddles proceedings with her confident delivery, layering her voice into jazzy, R&B inflected key changes that keep you guessing. Imagine an astral plane answer to Dawn Richard's ambient-inflected pop and you'll have some idea of where this is headed.

Then 'Dream 2' takes an unexpected diversion, the vocals replaced by swirling harp flourishes and the kind of floating synth stabs that draw a core logic from classic Ambient - Harold Budd, Laraaji et al - then adding extra colors just where necessary. And on 'Dream 3', faint, almost folk-y strings enter the frame, calling out from beyond the horizon, almost blotted out by a synth part that's in the thrall of Gigi Masin's legendary 'Clouds' - the track that ended up being repurposed by Björk on 'It's In Our Hands'. Zsela, Katz and Aged keep that momentum for the final track, too, letting cinematic strings echo around subtle synths and vanishing rhythms, hitting those hypnagogic, tranquil notes that so much contemporary ambient music seems to avoid. 'Cause at its heart, '4 Dreams' is deeper than that, a record that's entrenched in jazz, soul and classical minimalism rather than throwaway numbing music, of the contemporary varierty.

items.body:
David Tibet reawakens his landmark ’84 debut, proper, as Current 93; a primordial stew of tape loops, atonal electronics, blood curdle exhortations and altogether ill-willed heck on the A-side, countered by a flip of more sepulchral spatialisation and a bewitching Annie Anxiety that calves off into the abyss, all captured during a time when they lived in a squat and danced with Youth at goth crucible, The Batcave. Sacred stuff for anyone into NWW, earliest Coil / Zos Kia, Psychic TV...

"Current 93’s first and last album, NATURE UNVEILED dragged together my obsessions, as I had decided to make a pop album that dealt with my (then—as now!) primary fascinations: Christian apocalyptic and eschatological Christian texts. In my Speed-Ridden Soul and Mind, I thought I was reinventing The Ronettes, and that the 2 long sides of NATURE UNVEILED were A- and B- Sides of a Wall Of Soundhogs HIT! But the reality is that I was sharing a squat in Vauxhall with Little Annie Anxiety, and hanging out with Youth in The BatCave, with chickens rescued by The Animal Liberation Front in our backyard. Or did that come soon after, soon later? The album was recorded at The Roundhouse Studios in London’s Chalk Farm, home of Bronze Records, the label of my heroes (then—as now!) Uriah Heep, and Motörhead too, for whom I had moved stage-gear on their tour promoting their debut single on Chiswick Records. Anyway, anyway—I had not reinvented The Ronettes, though every time, every place, I listen to NATURE UNVEILED it Hits.

- David Tibet, Hastings, 11 March 2026."

If you're into Peter Brötzmann, Glenn Branca, John Zorn or Joe McPhee, consider it required listening. items.body:
If the casual's choice is 'A Love Supreme', the head's favorite has to be Coltrane's game-changing free jazz masterpiece 'Ascension', which Verve now presents remastered from the original tapes, in a complete edition featuring both explosive takes. If you're into Peter Brötzmann, Glenn Branca, John Zorn or Joe McPhee, consider it required listening.

Coltrane didn't invent free jazz - that was Ornette Coleman, who coined the term on his landmark 1960 album - but he certainly helped the New York City-centric movement gain an extra level of respectability when he released 'Ascension' in 1966. Because just a year prior, he'd released his most successful album ever, 'A Love Supreme', perfecting the post-bop/spiritual jazz sound he'd been refining for the last few years. At this stage, he was one of the most recognisable figures in jazz, certainly the most critically acclaimed, so his opinion held unimaginable weight. And unlike onlookers who saw Coleman and Albert Ayler as cacophonous noise, Coltrane was fascinated; he cites Coleman specifically as a direct influence and had been orbiting Ayler in the months before recording 'Ascension', scouring the East Coast for young players who might have the chops to keep up with his ideas. He picked fellow horn players Pharoah Sanders, Marion Brown, John Tchicai and Archie Shepp, trumpet players Dewey Johnson and Freddie Hubbard, bassists Jimmy Garrison and Art Davis, pianist McCoy Tyner and drummer Elvin Jones - all of whom are now household names.

And the group entered the Van Gelder Studio in New Jersey on June 28th 1965 without rehearsing beforehand. They recorded two sessions and weren't sure what to make of it at first. Even Coltrane admits he was overwhelmed at the time, worried about how it might be received and worked half to death. And when the album was released, despite its acclaim, Coltrane still wasn't sure; the second take of the day had been used, so a new edition was released labeled 'Ascension (Edition II)', using the first take. But it's splitting hairs, really - both takes capture Coltrane at the height of his powers as both a performer and a bandleader. Not only was he able to assemble some of the scene's most passionate, skillful players and corral them into refining a sound that hadn't yet been properly codified, he recorded one of the jazz scene's most volatile, influential and enduring avant-garde sets, an album that braided history with modernity and Black American culture with ideas informed by Coltrane's deep knowledge of African, Asian and Indian musical forms.

It's one of those records that's no doubt easier to digest now, six decades after its original release. 'Ascension' is still uncompromisingly eccentric, but its innovations have at the very least informed the direction of the avant vernacular, inspiring later jazz fusion experiments, noise artists, even certain strains of post-punk. And with a new remaster from Sterling Sound's Ryan K. Smith, it's really never sounded better. Timeless shit, really.

items.body:
Mor Elian's first vinyl release on Fever AM since 2022, 'Built In Waves' is a taut set of dancefloor-ready house psychedelia that never overlooks the importance of bass.

Elian's got a reputation to uphold. Not only has she blessed her Fever Am label with some of its most memorable bangers - just check 'Double Dip' or its predecessor 'Diva Test' - but she moved into a different zone entirely last year when she released her debut album 'Solid Space', forming weightless ambient textures to hover between the frenetic rhythms. 'Built In Waves' is a comeback of sorts, then, that re-affirms her dedication to the dancefloor, with a selection of four techy, twitchy bangers that'll do the job whether you're in Berlin or Bogatá. 

The title track welds brain-tickling synths and Errorsmith-like vocaloid effects over skittering, syncopated percussion that Elian routinely interrupts with hand drums, constantly sculpting the low-end into a pulsing, momentous thud. And the cheeky 'Get Ready With Me' is even better, a jittery 'Spastik' tribute at first that Elian wakes up with rasping 'Flat Beat'-style bass before the EP concludes with the Panorama Bar-ready ass shaker 'Ondulations'.

items.body:
London/Helsinki label Cold Blow map the subliminal links of early ‘90s electro, techno and its backroom, downbeat offshoots thru a plethora of tunes recorded ’92-’99 by the likes of Stasis, 2000 And One, CiM, all displaying how they translated Detroit techno intricacies and new age ambient soul for UK & EU bodies in motion, or those eaten by sofas.

“Across eight carefully selected slices of starry-eyed machine soul, Cold Blow presents an exquisite tour through backroom techno and downtempo electro. With a focus on thematic flow and an immersive listening experience, the London-based label explores works from leading lights of the 1990s and previously unreleased cuts that celebrate the human heart that can be discovered in synthetic sound practices.

The development of techno in the 1990s saw the music evolve in different directions across the world. From the expressive blueprint laid out by the Detroit pioneers, a wide range of tempos and energies emerged. Techno's evocative synthesis and intricate drum machine programming was especially potent for deeper explorations away from the dancefloor.

Documents Of Different Reality casts back to when technology was steering quantum leaps in communication and creativity and the future was shot through with naive optimism. It was also a time when the media and industry hadn't caught up with the music to box it into distinct categories. As such, there's a sense of creative freedom that informs the older tracks on the album, from 2000 And One and Sandy Huner's (originally as Pure) sparkling example of early Dutch techno to London-based LA Synthesis' detailed take on braindance and the majestic night sky vision of cult legend Stasis.

There's also space for rare, late 90s machine funk from Icelandic outlier Thor alongside Connective Zone's charmingly fractured bleep dream and a more contemporary offering from Barcelona-based duo Permutation. Meanwhile Mind Control and CiM both capture the spirit of stylistic fusion with twitchier rhythms that take influence from hardcore and jungle as much as techno.

With an atmospheric through-line of melancholic pads and harmonious leads, this small but perfectly formed collection naturally follows on from previous, equally thought-out compilations on Cold Blow, and adds a distinct perspective on the history and continuing legacy of pioneering early ambient techno.”

items.body:
Indonesian instrument-builder and folk mutator Johanes “Mo’ong” Santoso Pribadi meets wildman Shigeru Ishihara (aka Scotch Rolex) on a 2nd Takkak Takkak screwball for Nyege Nyege Tapes, tipped FFO Gabber Modus Operandi, Hulubalang, Raja Kirik, Lord Spikeheart.

One up to the duo’s eponymous debut of 2024, the possessed tempest of ‘Abu’ opens wormhole portals to fantasy dimensions triangulated with frightening vibrancy. The 40 minute trip goes hard into sweltering zones where ancient folk rituals encounter modern technology and psyches, replete with shifting atmospheric conditions and febrile oneiric logic. The results are a hyperrealistic projection of heck, taking listeners by the scruff of the neck and plunging them into an anomalous sort of fantasy island or parallel world teeming with phosphorescent life, from the animalcule level to the metaphysical. 

The ceremonial atmosphere of opening track 'Hai no uta' mixes Javanese gong with flute blasts  interspersed with unsettling electronic vibrations, while the title track takes shape through hoarse chants and a cocktail of rhythms: tuned, gamelan-like resonances through ordered electro-plated taiko structures, evolving into fractured free improv and syrupy drone metal. The album keeps shifting through these tense ceremonial sounds and hard dance textures, inviting heavy electronic kicks into the mannered mass of flutes and metallophone, matching acoustic instrumentation with carnivalesque synths and hardstyle rhythms.

Get your imaginary jabs in: it’s wild out there.

items.body:
Airbrushed, subtropical, new age ambient-jazz from Jesse Peterson’s Maui-based project, given its highest profile platform to date on Amsterdam’s Music From Memory, and warmly advised to admirers of his regular spars, Carlos Niño, Laraaji, Mia Doi Todd...

"Originally formed in New York in the late 2000s, Turn On The Sunlight has evolved into a fluid, location-spanning practice rooted in collaboration, intuition and process. Now based on Maui, Peterson’s work draws together a wide network of musicians and environments, with recordings taking shape across Los Angeles, Tokyo, London, San Miguel de Allende and Haʻikū.

Loosely situated within a framework of organic, ambient-leaning jazz, 'Iseo' unfolds as a series of open, exploratory pieces, with electronics sitting subtly beneath acoustic and environmental elements. Built from layered instrumentation including synthesizers, guitar, zither, flutes, voice and field recordings, Peterson moves between grounded, tactile detail and more expansive, immersive states. A sense of warmth and permeability runs throughout: organic percussion, environmental textures and drifting rhythmic elements lend the record a gently saturated humidity, reflecting Peterson’s base in Hawaii, where the presence of nature is felt as much as it is heard.

Underlying the project is a way of working rooted in gathering, listening and tending. Instruments, ensemble sessions, field recordings and everyday environments are approached with attentiveness, shaped through collecting, refining and allowing things to settle. Relationships, landscape and lived experience shape the sound, giving 'Iseo' a tactile, almost hand-made quality.

Rather than fixed arrangements, the album feels as if it has been organically and lovingly assembled through a process of listening and response, each element finding its place within a wider, evolving whole. This approach reaches a natural centre point in the 15-minute piece 'Medianoche En La Calle Aurora', which unfolds patiently, bending through shifting environments as motifs and textures emerge and dissolve with quiet continuity.

Peterson’s role as both instigator and facilitator is central to the project. Bringing together a diverse group of collaborators including Carlos Niño, Mia Doi Todd, Laraaji, Ko Ishikawa, Luis Pérez Ixoneztli and Miles Spilsbury, he creates space for individual voices to emerge within a shared language. The result is a music defined by openness and generosity.

'Iseo' takes its title from Peterson’s son’s middle name, a word that can be understood to mean ‘one-world life’. The piece itself takes the form of a gentle lullaby, its melody loosely shaped around the syllables of his name and sung to Peterson’s son by Luis Pérez Ixoneztli, a close collaborator whose presence across the record reflects a long-standing relationship that extends beyond the music itself.

Sleeve art and design by Michael Willis."

items.body:
Really feeling this trippy acid treat by a one-of-a-kind Lolina; her 10th solo album since the last Hype Williams drop with Dean Blunt in the early 2010s, and typically riddled with low-key mischievous slants on mutant dance-pop, as heard in her regular midweek club night at ace London venue, Spanners.

Chasing up her trip-hop tinted LP ‘Unrecognisable’ (2024), and a mix CD as Balmainjeans repping her club night ‘Distressed’, Lolina plays to an ideally unpredictable form with a shift into acid pop on ‘Monopoly of Mistakes’; featuring eleven concentrated formulations of dry drum machines x tweakiest 303 gunk gilded with those vocals that keep us coming back. The combo of silver box x slanted vox finds the DIY prism-pusher bending timelines thru lo-fi indie-pop with sound system steppas, basement noise, cold wave and free party acid tekno, but never quite settling into any one style.

Maintaining her mutable range of variations within a theme, Monopoly of Mistakes really catches our breath with the way Lolina turns a paucity of ingredients into a dead satisfying thing. Whether commanding the 303 to the beat-less abstraction ‘Border Beach’ or alloying with wooziest keys and steppas fizz on ‘The Mercenaries’, or going deep into the lushest wormhole on the titular, 7 minute standout, her min-to-max sense of economy is key to this LP’s appeal. It’s there in the piquant synth-pop of ‘Menace’ and ‘Everlasting’ - think Wee Papa Girl Rappers via Dave Ball at John T. Gast’s - and calling to mind a lost SOPHIE x EVOL gem in ’Stand Off’. But it’s also finely measured with an utterly gorgeous new age miniature harking to classic Hype Williams on ‘Welcome to the Drift of Whats Already Begun’, and of course the zinging closer ‘Penalty’, where zippiest ‘80s french cold wave meets AFXian harmony and a sort of Dopplereffektish science-lab engineering in a chef’s kiss demo of the extended melodic wooo that sets all her work apart.

Best believe it’s fully distinctive, addictive gear.

items.body:
Slamming, sci-fi skooled Detroit jit from the sound’s contemporary standard bearer, bolstered by a lethal Arpanet remix from Gerald Donald, whose early Dopplereffekt classics are ghettotech/jit canon.

On four brisk originals Shawscape Renegade weaves extramusical inspiration from classic sci-fi themes - existential dread; the costs of technological evolution; the dead ends of overspecialisation - into tightly coiled club motors. 

His acidic electrofunked ’78 Light Years From Earth’ pings like a Stingray zinger, and ‘Mechanise 9’ locks into a proper pneumatic 4/4 pump galvanised with gunky synths, and ‘Ignition One’ pares it all back to fluid bass hydrodynamic punctuated by the type of snares that knock your fillings out - as deployed in the Black to Techno documentary soundtrack. 

His ‘Terraformers Warning’ is a standout of inimitable 313 machine funk, but let’s be fair, Arpanet’s Quanta Remodel of the same components is just on a whole nexx level: riddled with breathless detailing, discordant synth voices and cyber-dubbed aerodynamic sleekness that will sound utterly sick on a decent rig. 

DJs beware - “the vinyl versions of A1 & B1 are five BPM slower than the digital, moving the music to between 128BPM and 151BPM on a standard Technics turntable and opening it up for play in a greater range of club environs.

items.body:
Back by demand - 2nd hand copies are known to trade for triple figures - Cindy’s timeless suite of sexy, hazed dream-pop is acutely tipped to anyone who holds a flame for Julee Cruise, Voice Actor, Lynch, Enya, Bianca Scout, Vince Clarke...

‘I’m Cindy’ is a chef’s kiss of effortlessly slow, seductive lo-fi songwriting that practically smushes earlobes with its heavenly marriage of Kai Hugo's faded production lustre and singer, Blue LoLãn’s range of whispered sweet nothings and harmonised coos. In the years since its original release it’s taken on a life of its own as a go-to succour for lovers of blissed-out, cinematic waft with equal measures of soft-focus, nostalgic FM synths and details that caress and crack in all the right, tender places. 

Conceptually derived from Palmbomen II’s ‘Memories of Cindy’ session of 2017, the 13 tracks find marbled whorls of sensual fascination within that LP’s fantasy reminiscence, here expanded into a spectrum of LA-via-Antwerp dream-pop like Johnny Jewel meets Alex Zhang Hungtai on the synth and sax pearl ‘Another’ or lip-smacking cruiser ‘Justin’, thru a Voice Actor-esque ‘Voice Message’ and the gossamer FM synth fronds that wrap it up on ‘Maybe Because It’s Over Now’, whilst secreting shimmers of Vince Clarke ballads in ‘2y & 6m’, and acid-laced lo-fi machine crack shades away from Maria Minerva on ’Never Let Me Go’.

No brainer!

items.body:
Flautist and composer Taiga Ultan joins the Kou Records roster with one of the most chilling solo flute records we've heard, recorded as usual in high def by the great Randall Dunn.

The flute is one of those instruments that's terminally misunderstood. Ancient and beautiful, it's often marginalized as a solo voice, even though it's been used in that way for quite literally thousands of years. Ultan seems to understand its historical resonance as she tracks through 'Shade Zero'. On opener 'Adagio', she acknowledges its place in classical music, offering up a virtuosic performance, but as the album creeps on, her playing is freed up, her tone more unsettling. Just listening to 'Act I', where she creates animalistic sounds and percussive flurries with the flute's keys, or 'Act II', where the instrument is turned into a vessel for her screams. 

When she introduces spoken language in the album's back half, it seems to affirm Ultan's relationship with the instrument, oddly enough. The flute is always there, but there's no sound without a voice. "Why do I think the thoughts that I think," she muses on 'Neighbors' over rainfall. The flute appears again on 'Memorial Day', but the sound has changed, dipped to an owl like hoot in the distance, way behind Ultan's words.

items.body:
A leading light of neo-ambient takes their maiden bow on Glasgow’s stealthily expansive co:clear label after cherished turns with the sferic and Stroom labels.

The International Billionaire’s Love Child, or tiblsc for brevity, is the avatar of a Leipzig-based artist in possession of a distinctive, world-building ambient purview that has clearly stroked a nerve for listeners chasing the modern ambient zeitgeist, especially their couplet of ‘Delusive Tongue Shifts - Situation Based Compositions’ (2021) + ‘Hypertranslucent’ (2022). Those albums’ careful bends of pulpy sentiment and intricate, immersively dreamlike architecture is now echoed in ‘City of Something’, where her tender feel for compression and blends of HD and lo-fi tones fosters a gauzy sense of depth perception and sonorous emotional resonance. 

More so than her previous work, the eight tracks here are laced with a flickering pop spirit that riddles the album’s finely meshed dimensions, calling to mind aspects of Perila that are whisked to its most elegant frisson in ‘Resting Bitch Face’, or catching breathy contrails of an airspun pop song in ‘The Sun Really Is Something Round’, whilst tickling private parts of the imagination with the compressed artefacts of ‘You Just Want’, edging on Shinetiac’s take on smudged sheogaze trip hop in ‘Scare Me’, and teasing the most elusive urges on a secretive, quietly restive closer ‘Until the End of Time’.

items.body:
Surf Gang co-founder Eera comes correct on his first solo album, trading brittle cloud rap for squashed trance and tempered EDM and connecting with Mechatok, Nick León and CRUSH3d in the process.

If you didn't know by now, Surf Gang aren't your average rap production outfit. Evilgiane is regularly seen on underground festival bills, playing back-to-back with Evian Christ or palling around with Skrillex, while Harrison decided to go the atmospheric route on his solo debut 'Taking a walk & calling a car home', following his production on 'POMPEII // UTILITY' with a sequence of moody instrumentals. Cameron Kozloff, better known as Eera, takes a different route entirely, following the undercurrent of blown-out, saccharine dance music that's flourishing on YouTube, TikTok and Bandcamp if you're prepared to look beyond the anime artwork and videogame references.

Really, what Eera's isolated is that rap and contemporary trance have plenty in common - Araabmusik wasn't heading down a creative dead end when he released 'Electronic Dream' all those years ago. And 'Just Keep Holding On' sounds impressively plugged in; it's packed out with zeitgeist-y themes that might as well have been snatched from a PS2-era RPG (just check 'I Know' and prepare to weep) and features some unexpected guest appearances. León assists on 'Just Being Honest', a romantic, whimsical track that mutates into Daft Punk-like electro house and Berlin's Mechatok mucks in for lead single 'Sad But So Funny', a Robert Miles-alike piano-led banger.

items.body:
LA jazz+ quintet SML crystallise fresh forms of spiky, motorik, expansive takes on the space between spiritual jazz, electric Miles Davis fusions, Reichian minimalism and the lithe funk of Afrobeat or Can, for an effusive debut on staple Chicago label, International Anthem

“'Spontaneous Music Live' contains two side-length pieces of unedited improvisation, recorded live at Los Angeles venue Zebulon during SML's December 2025 three-night residency, just weeks after the release of the band's second album HOW YOU BEEN. It was recorded and mixed live to analog tape by Bryce Gonzales (the same engineer/wizard known for his gorgeous live captures/mixes of Jeff Parker's ETA IVtet).

Between HOW YOU BEEN and their 2024 debut SMALL MEDIUM LARGE (both of which were heavily edited, shaped and post-produced) the band has developed a reputation for records that are heavily fused, polished, and punchy. The medium is on full post-modern display on those LPs, and the band’s post-production knife can be responsible for much of the perspective — the tastiest morsels collected, arranged, and rearranged just so.

But the source material from both those albums were live recordings. Long-form, unwieldy, ebbing and flowing. On top of that, every performance the band has ever done has been fully improvised in that spirit. So in the sphere of live performance the band’s esteem has grown down a different path — one of linear, hypnotic, expansion. It’s a perceived split persona shared by some of SML’s most inspiring conceptual bedfellows: compare the extended madness of Can’s 'Live in Paris 1973' to the relative tight form of 'Future Days' from the same year; the speed-funk chaos of Miles Davis’ 'Dark Magus' to the heavily deconstructed 'On The Corner' or 'Big Fun'.

'Spontaneous Music Live' removes the curatorial perspective and pulls the curtain back on that search-pluck-reconstruct editing process. What we’re left with is the psychedelic realism of the band in situ, in their home town, collectively improvising, fully in-the-moment, mining for that moment of discovery. We hear, in macro, each nugget of sound which could be the basis for a future SML album track, spattered amongst the collective chaos-and-control like stars in the night sky.”

items.body:
Mexican sound artist Concepción Huerta presents a carefully crafted new album - "both a tribute to the literary work of Eduardo Galeano and a howl from the Lacandon jungle in Mexico".

"This album, crafted entirely on a subharmonic framework and meticulously processed through tape manipulation, stands as Concepción Huerta’s sharpest work to date, undoubtedly her most abrasive, intense, and exhilarating. Her signature remains intact: an approach deeply rooted in drone, musique concrète, and hauntingly visceral textures.

Conceptually, Huerta’s sonic vision evokes an image of open veins, not human veins, but those of the earth itself, the open veins of Latin America. These nervures are, in truth, rivers of lava; fury transmuted into fire coursing beneath the land until it erupts. The album is, in a way, a reflection on dispossession, resource extraction, and colonization. But beyond being a historical commentary—one that some might relegate to a forgotten past—it is also a reminder of the present, of how these practices persist in contemporary, postmodern guises.

It serves as both a tribute to the literary work of Eduardo Galeano, one of the most influential voices of Latin American leftist thought, and a howl from the Lacandon jungle in Mexico, resonating with the Zapatista struggle, the resistance of the Guaraní people in Paraguay and Argentina, and the voices of Indigenous communities across Latin America.

In the 16th century, a book titled Visión de los vencidos (The Broken Spears) was published in Mexico, compiling Nahuatl texts that presented the unofficial history, the account of the defeated. Concepción Huerta’s album El Sol de los Muertos (The Sun of the Dead) is not a call to action nor a reactionary manifesto, but an invitation to reflection, a historical reexamination. It urges us not to accept the official narrative at face value and serves as a warning, to remain vigilant and, within our capacities, resist the resurgence of fascism and colonialism in all its modern forms.

Recorded by Concepción Huerta in 2024 between Berlin, The Hague, and Mexico City. Volcano photography by Magaly Ugarte. Mastered by Rafael Anton Irisarri at Black Knoll Studio, New York. The tapes were duplicated in Avranches, France, and the cover was risograph printed in Barcelona by Mateo Barbuzzi aka Club del Prado. Design by Daniel Castrejón in Mexico City."

items.body:
Essential listening FFO Time Is Away, Jon Collin or the 'Bagpuss' soundtrack, Rory Salter, aka Malvern Brume, confronts cutesy British folk nostalgia on 'For Red Riverbank', using 'The Wind in the Willows' references, sobering newsreel snippets and straight-to-tape acoustic jams to develop a faded image of labour inequality.

Nostalgia is supposed to be digestible - a cultural banana that gives the mind all familiarity without friction. But munch on the same gear for too long and it starts to cause irritation; it's hard not to notice, for example, that the prim Ghost Box-style Gen Z hauntology has reached its logical conclusion. Whatever it was saying about the UK's welfare-era lost futures has not only been photocopied half to death, but it's also been added to the slop machine, spat out as empty "content" that's almost hypnotically nauseating - especially when you consider the state of welfare in 2026. Thankfully, we're not the only people to have noticed; Salter takes aim at the romance of British folk culture on his proper The Sprigs debut, using a framework we'll all be familiar with - Kenneth Grahame's Edwardian children's classic 'The Wind in the Willows'. It's important to note that the book was already steeped in nostalgia when it was first published back in 1908, a reflection on nature in the face of mass industrialization, as the affordable Ford Model T was beginning to appear on roads for the first time. So it's a more complex reference than you might initially figure, and Salter uses this backdrop to root his investigation of British labour history and the very meaning of tradition.

We've all heard remnants of folk music vibrate through the collective consciousness over the years, not least in the wake of the New Weird America movement of the early '00s. And Salter's awareness of these sounds and the perpetual churn that followed is crucial; he doesn't subvert them as such, but repurposes them, hitting on themes and sequences that connect us to the country's soil and textures that help to rub away some of nostalgia's entrancing sparkle. The 12-minute opener 'come along, back home' sounds at first like an old protestant hymn being bellowed through broken pipes and Salter keeps scraping away at history, collaging textured environmental loops with simplistic, almost naive folk songs, peculiar resonances and, occasionally, what sounds like an old recorder. And it's the back-and-forth between gravelly noise and nostalgic naivety that makes 'For Red Riverbank' so inviting. The short, sharp 'Ratty & the moles get to work' is just as jolly as its title, sounding as brittle and evocative as Sandra Kerr and John Faulkner's fluttered folk songs that lifted Oliver Postgate's 'Bagpuss'.

And Salter doesn't just look back through rose-tinted spectacles, he juxtaposes these evocative sounds with sobering recordings of newsreaders, politicians and union leaders, who complete a quite genuine picture of the recent past. Like George Eliot's Middlemarch, that imagined a fictional Midlands town four decades prior to its writing, the inviting idealized setting was a Trojan horse for Eliot's real theme: the 1832 Reform Act that upended the electoral system. Salter employs the same sleight of hand, introducing us to a world we know and love before drip, drip, dripping the politics we so desperately need.

items.body:
‘Aftersun’ composer Coates furnishes a score of heart-in-mouth classical strings, keys and choral arrangements to gay romance flick ‘Pillion’, aka an opportunity to ogle Alexander Skarsgård, replete with biker leathers, in a sub-dom relationship

By now one of the preeminent composers in his field - up there with Mica Levi, 0PN, Bobby Krlic et al - Coates continues to expand and hone his distinctly classic yet fresh palette and chops to purpose on this particularly lush set of orchestrations and sweeping sound design, including his take on a Satie evergreen. Gently gelled to the film’s narrative, revolving a shy yung queer lad seduced into a BDSM relationship with a dashing local biker, Coates’ score is ravishingly sensual and heady, full of oneiric allusions to classical, ambient, lavish ballads and twinkling electronica, all sure to hit pleasure centres of anyone who fancies Romance, Jonny Greenwood’s ‘Phantom Thread’ OST, Enya’s crushed velvet wafters, or event schmaltziest ends of Leyland Kirby.

items.body:
Following 2024's avant-prog-Americana song cycle 'Viewfinder', guitar deity Wendy Eisenberg goes chamber pop on their self-titled latest, tipping their hat to Judee Sill, Gillian Welch, Van Dyke Parks and Joanna Newsom.

When they relocated from rural Western Mass to Brooklyn in 2020, Eisenberg was hit with a wave of longing for the open landscape they'd left behind. They were drawn to classic country and folk records, perfectly poised offerings from Willie Nelson and John Hartford and lavish pop-folk records from Jimmy Webb and Van Dyke Parks as well as the weirdo fare of Richard Dawson et al. So when 'Viewfinder', a way of deconstructing the experience following eye surgery in 2011, was finished, Eisenberg started writing "genuinely folk songs" and swapping out their usually showy, complex performance for a form of relative simplicity that they explain is inherently strange all the same. Prog becomes folk, basically. And they're not on their own; more eaze handles the lush string arrangements, playing pedal steel and synthesizer, and a loose band forms around that axis, with drummer Ryan Sawyer and bassist Trevor Dunn.

But despite the personnel, it's resolutely Eisenberg's album. Their voice sounds unrestrained, capturing the era they're referencing and their own emotional (and physical upheaval). It's fragile but strangely warm on the country-tinged Jim O'Rourke-like 'Will You Dare' and hypnotic on the baroque 'Meaning Business', a track they wrote in the wake of David Lynch's death as the antithesis of the "Lynchian" aesthetic. And they should really get their flowers for this one; Americana, especially now, is teetering on a precipice, almost knocked off the edge by half-assed, churned attempts and underwritten pastiches. Eisenberg's an attentive listener and someone who's surrounded themself with similarly sensitive ears, people who are able to fill their heart and their sound so what we hear is as byzantine as a Gastr del Sol record but sounds as effortless as John Prine's 'Angel From Montgomery'. If you loved Joanna Newsom's 'Ys' and have never found anything quite as satisfying, this is the one.

items.body:
One of the most distinctive and legendary vocal/dub albums of all time, recorded in 1981 by the “dub dentist” Keith Hudson, ‘Playing It Cool & Playing It Right’ is now back in circulation for the first time in over 20 years, when it was first given overdue flowers via Basic Channel And Honest Jon’s ‘Basic Replay’ programme. It still burns with a rare energy, making it an untouchable, foundational text for the ages.

Keith Hudson (1946-1984) was one of dub reggae’s most distinctive innovators, renowned for a run of classic solo albums and productions for U-Roy, Big Youth, Ken Boothe and Horace Andy between 1972 and his untimely passing in 1984. However, Hudson's late period is where the real imperial juice can be found, a time that saw him move from Jamaican to London and New York studios, applying his unfathomable production style to a heavily americanised strain of vocal Soul. ‘Playing It Cool & Playing It Right’ is the pinnacle of that late period, an album that builds layer upon layer of alchemical brilliance.

Hudson’s combination of hooks and complex, highly unusual production is really unlike anything else from the period, or since, crooning in a soul mode made more haunting by a discreetly judicious application of tape FX, endlessly heavy subs, and mixing desk tricks deployed to delirious, almost psycho-acoustic effect.  The album was originally meant to feature one of Hudson's teenage sons to voice the dubs, but in the event the Love Joys, Wayne Jarrett, and inimitably Hudson himself featured at the microphone, with the dozen cuts co-produced by Wackies founder Lloyd ‘Bullwackie’ Barnes - the only collaboration between the two producers. It was originally issued on Hudson’s own label, Joint International, with subsequent pressings on Basic Replay in 2003, making it increasingly sought-after in the years since. 

Alongside reggae’s first concept album, ‘Flesh of My Skin, Blood of My Blood’, ‘Playing It Cool’ remains one the genre’s most important and unusual releases, picking up new disciples with every new wave of listeners taken aback by its stark, brooding blooze and brittle, spectral rendering.

items.body:
Electronic Corporation "1998–2006", a compilation bringing together rare and long unavailable recordings by the German electronic projects heimelektronik and MAS 2008.

"Active around the turn of the millennium, both projects share the involvement of producer Ive Müller while developing distinct collaborations and approaches to electronic music. H.E.I.M. Elektronik was founded in 1996 by Holger Erlenwein and Ive Müller (after the two artists split in 1999, Müller continued using the name), while MAS 2008 is the project of Ive Müller together with René Kirchner. Though separate entities, the two projects explored a similar sonic territory: stripped-down electro, minimal electronics and machine-driven body music shaped by analog hardware and a raw DIY production ethos.

The roots of Müller’s work go back to the final years of the DDR. As a teenager he worked as a licensed DJ — officially known as a “Schallplattenunterhalter” — operating a travelling disco across Saxony. With limited access to official Western releases, music circulated through cassette recordings taped from West German radio stations such as RIAS Berlin, NDR2 and Bayern3. Together with friends he travelled between youth clubs and discos around Leipzig with a “rolling discotheque”: a Russian Wolga pulling a trailer loaded with Electro-Voice sound systems sourced through the black market.

At the turn of the 2000s this background in underground electronic culture resurfaced in a series of recordings rooted in electro, EBM and minimal machine music. The tracks collected on Electronic Corporation 2000–2002 capture this moment: cold sequences, driving rhythms and stark synthetic textures produced with a direct and uncompromising approach.

Compiled and remastered by Rude 66 from the original sources, Electronic Corporation 2000–2002 documents a small but fascinating chapter of German underground electronics from the early digital era."

Minimalist, uncompromising, and inspired by krautrock, punk, new wave, elect
items.body:
44 years after its original release, the 7” by German group DEUTSCHE SCHÄFERHUNDE (engl. German shepherds) - remastered and reissued for the first time on Anna Logue Records.

"Recorded in the winter of 1981/82 between rehearsal space, provincial disco and bar nights, and a humble four-track setup, these tracks capture the raw spirit of a generation that simply started creating—no formal training, but plenty of attitude. Minimalist, uncompromising, and inspired by krautrock, punk, new wave, electronic music and dub, the songs move between raw electronics, percussive noise, new wave experimentation, and sharp social commentary. „Rosa Brille“ (rose coloured glasses) in particular feels as urgent today as it did back then—a track that has lost none of its relevance, „Gasmasken“ tells of gas masks dancing in the woods to the sound of sirens, and a timeless Holger Czukay/Jah Wobble inspired „Mein Herz“ (my heart).

Originally pressed in a small run of just 500 copies and later becoming a sought-after collector’s item now worth 200€, the record now returns in a carefully crafted edition featuring a laser-printed reverse side and additional materials such as original lyric sheets and articles, postcard and poster. DEUTSCHE SCHÄFERHUNDE thrived on paradox—a provocative name paired with a clear stance, and lyrics that still resonate today. Shaped by Cold War tension, political unease, and youthful rebellion, their sound refused to fit into any neat category. Only few other bands, such as Der Musikant, Im Namen des Volkes, Thorax Wach, Klinisch Sauber oder Stephan Eicher spielt Noise Boys come to mind."

items.body:
Modular bod M. Geddes Gengras gets the band back together on 'Guestlist', roping in an estimable team of collaborators (including Christina Carter, WANDA GROUP, Greg Fox, Ben Chasny and Meg Duffy, among others) to recapture the lightning in a bottle energy of Chicago's early post-rock era, when sounds would criss-cross over each other relatively freely.

Despite technology being accessible, commonplace even, it's still relatively difficult to find the sweet spot between live instrumentation and electronics. Modular synthesis, that thrives on its self-contained, often unpredictable moments of serendipity, adds an even more problematic element. You can make it work, sure, but so much of what we like about modular music is that it doesn't feel as if it's been looped into structures that file down its sharp edges. Gengras sets himself a challenge here, working like a synthesist but also drawing on his experience playing in bands - he sees both sides, which gives him a head-start. And he's also got the good sense to think back to an era where the possibilities felt endless: the "early Pro Tools" era as James Toth writes in the accompanying notes, when bands like Tortoise and The Sea and Cake were looking at artists like Autechre and AFX and wondering what techniques they could integrate.

And 'Guest List' is undoubtedly Gengras' most ambitious record to date. There's more to it than personnel, too - proper songs, a far cry from the hazy new age-tinted synth jams that we heard on 'Expressed, I Noticed Silence' or the post-kosmische "ROMpler worship" of 'QUIK-MELT', appear in the dense tangle of instruments and expressions. While the 11-minute 'The List is Millions Long' initially seems to not-so-subtly reference Tortoise's 'Millions Now Living...' with its chiming guitars and motorik beat (supplied by Portland-based sound artist Colin Blanton, no less), it gets more complicated when Will Epstein's saxophone enters the frame. And that harmonic complexity remains when the track melts into 'Laplace/Montagne' and Gengras' synth belches are augmented by Chasny's golden shreds. Hell, there are even vocals on 'Seven Dials' provided by Austin's Cory Plump, who shouts listlessly over Gengras' sunny arpeggios, Fox's drums and Duffy's riffs.

Prepare yourself, 'Guest List' is not the M. Geddes Gengras you're likely to be expecting. There's even a spoken word intro to the album's brilliant finale '"The Weather"' from cult social media star and sometime genius WANDA GROUP. Proper good.

items.body:
Real heart-stopping, life-affirming, almost indescribably beautiful posthumous album featuring (for the first time) vocal works by beloved, dearly departed, Ethiopian nun and now-legendary pianist/composer Emahoy Tsege Mariam Gebru, room recorded straight to tape between 1977-1985, sounds of life just about audible in the background. Almost had an out of body experience listening to it the other night - just a perfect, 10/10 album.

’Souvenirs’ is an intimate self-portrait written, recorded and compiled by the late Emahoy Tsege Mariam Gebru; a classically-trained pianist turned nun, whose singular style of jazz and blues-inflected composition and performance became globally renowned in her latter years via reissues and compilations reaching as far back as the 1960s, namely the ‘Éthiopiques 21: Piano Solo’ CD and a much-prized eponymous set in 2016. At the age of 99, Emahoy passed away in Jerusalem last year, whilst planning towards this first ever showcase of her vocals - which have never appeared on her purely piano-based recordings until now, making for a truly life-affirming experience from its opening bars. 

The posthumous release, realised in collaboration with Emahoy’s family and Mississippi Records - is a stone cold stunner. It grants unprecedented access to her discrete craft and inner world in Addis Ababa, against a backdrop of the Ethiopian Red Terror and Civil War, prior to her subsequent exile in a Jerusalem convent. Whilst all no doubt defined by her signature, intricate and lilting type of classical meets jazz-blues phrasing, the eight songs are all far more concise than her usual instrumental works, made even more spellbinding by the revelation of her softly contoured and captivating vocals that beautifully trace and overlie the cadence of her keys. It’s just pure, unbridled expression that’s only heightened by the seemingly off-the-cuff nature of the recordings, as if she just sung the songs to herself, impromptu, never intended for public consumption.

Replete with incidental creaks of the piano stool, birds outside the window, and Emahoy’s finger on the record button, the songs depict themes of loss, mourning and soon-to-be exile, sung into a basic boombox. They place us in the room with her, closer than ever, privy to a vocal version of the closing number to her eponymous compilation, now unveiled as a dedication her niece, the titular Tenkou, with lyrics to guide her adulthood “Don’t cry / Childhood won’t come back / Let it go with love”, alongside the beatific, open-window paean ‘Clouds Moving on the Sky’, and melancholic hiraeth of ‘Ethiopia My Homeland’ or ‘Don’t Forget Your Country’, and ineffable, humbling elegance of idea and execution to ‘Is It Sunny or Cloudy in the Land You Live?’ and ‘Where is the Highway of Thought?’.

Unmissable.

items.body:
Danish composer Astrid Sonne opens up her heart on 'Great Doubt', singing candidly for the first time over powdery beats and jerky instrumentation (assisted by none other than Slauson Malone, Ben Vince, Levitation Orchestra's Emma Barnaby and Alvilda Reiter Jakobsen), and even referencing Mariah Carey. It's a revelation - and funny in places too - properly in line with Tirzah, ML Buch and HTRK.

We almost didn't recognize Sonne when we first spun 'Great Doubt'. Her voice - not her viola or rack of synths - takes the spotlight on 'Do you wanna', murmuring gently over brittle, tightly reverberating drums that Sonne plays herself. It's a far cry from the pitchy, jazz-inflected psychedelia of 2021's 'outside of your lifetime' or its vaporous predecessor 'Human Lines'. "Do you wanna have a baby?" she asks ruefully, leaving the question unanswered at first, room for strings, piano and subtle synths to reply. She strips herself naked, wondering what it might mean to bring a child into the world; it scrapes against Tirzah's 'Colourgrade' not just sonically but thematically. On that album, Tirzah contemplated motherhood and family - here, Sonne weighs up her choices, using the track's emptiness to suggest emotional malnutrition. "I don't know," she finally relents.

'Give my all' follows with boxy, disney strings and orchestral phrases that bring an uncanny drama to Sonne's blunt words. She sounds confident and forthright as she paraphrases Maria Carey: "I'd give my all to have / just one more night with you." The plasticity of the backdrop only makes the words resonate further, and it's this push and pull between artificiality and raw sensitivity that makes 'Great Doubt' so captivating. There's an unmistakable trip-hop impetus to 'Boost', that features Sonne on drums again, playing slowly alongside sampled woodwinds and fictile synths. There are no vocals on this one, so the instrumentation stands in, winding in and out of tune to poke out towards the boundaries. It's at this moment when Sonne sounds closest to her sometime collaborator ML Buch, bridging the gap between traditional songwriting and a simulated new age. But Sonne doesn't sound as if she's trying to approximate pop, just bare her soul more frankly.

And there are traces of her earlier material on the stand-out 'Staying here', when she coos more animatedly over organ-like arpeggios and digitized stabs. We can hear outlines of classic Enya or Kate Bush on this one, and while it's beatless, it sounds as if it's rushing towards a drop that never comes - all tension, no release. "Everything is unreal," she cries. "But I'm not going anywhere." Then we're led out with the folk-y 'Overture', that features Ben Vince on sax, and dubby closer 'Say you love me', the biggest indicator that she's now based in London. It's the most revealing, heart-puncturing material we've heard from Sonne to date, a hyper-literate wirework of influences and skills that's put together with care and no small amount of restraint. We're sold.

The Cave12 reco
items.body:
Lauded Canadian no wave noise rockers Earthball live by their improvised wits on convention-scything recordings made at Cave 12, Geneva, and Le Guess Who? Festival, The Netherlands.

"Side A captures a thumping performance at Cave12 in Geneva. Frazzled from a white-knuckle alpine descent, the group settles into a hypnotic sprawl, stretching time and form across a colossal 53-minute set (with the first 22 minutes presented on the LP; the full performance appears on the CD edition). The Cave12 recording is a study in tension and release; ruminative, volatile, and barely contained. Drums stumble and surge, saxophone howls cut through the air, and Ford and Van Wyke’s voices briefly pull together the circle twice, before the tumult lapses into a spinning maelstrom.

Side B meanwhile presents a scorched excerpt from EarthBall’s crushing performance at Le Guess Who? Festival. As Van Wyke reflects: “Having the most excellent Dwarfs of East Agouza play before us only heightened our intention to bring the noise. Listening back, the thing that strikes me most is how we truly were operating in the ever-elusive but always sought-after ‘group mind’. Ninety-degree changes are super tight. Izzy and I are finishing each other’s sentences. Liam’s horn is cradling our outer and inner space. Kellan’s talk box rains down like the voice of a reawakened spirit, and all this havoc is safely stowed in the rumbling ox-cart of John’s solid drumming”.

EarthBall are an avant/noise/rock wrecking ball of a band from Nanaimo, Canada. Rooted in total improvisation, free expression, and a deeply psychedelic sensibility, EarthBall operate on pure instinct. They hurtle onwards in a combustion of spontaneous composition, shooting from the hip, as they fall out of the sky ablaze. The group encompass Isabel Ford (vocals, bass), John Brennan (drums, percussion), Jeremy Van Wyke (vocals, guitar, trumpet), Kellan Maclaughlin (guitar, talkbox), and Liam Murphy (saxophone). Each member brings a rich and varied musical history, with past and present projects including Shearing Pinx, Plan Your Future, Kamikaze Nurse, Eschatons, and Psychedelic Dirt. Collectively and individually, they have collaborated with artists such as Deerhoof, Raven Chacon, Chris Corsano, and William Hooker, deepening the band’s exploratory reach and collective language.

Actual Earth Music - Volume 3 & 4 marks another ascent in EarthBall’s ever-expanding, totemic discography, an ecstatic storm of raw immediacy and unfiltered expression. EarthBall came, conjured and opened the portal! Blink and it’s gone. What was that? Actual Earth Music!"

items.body:
A more Manhattan than Manhattan itself blend of critic-friendly rock, snotty sleaze-punk and weed-headed loser rap, Chanel Beads' debut album is Dimes Square pressed to wax.

Helmed by engineer and musician Shane Lavers, Chanel Beads are indicative of a very contemporary wave of New York City-centric art and music; they're that side of the pond's bar italia, in other words. The difference is that 'Your Day Will Come' is innovative in its own way. Sure, there are traces to be found of Pitchfork-favored indie's past: NYC legends Gang Gang Dance and The Dirty Projectors, for example. But Lavers muddles his influences with references to Talk Talk, Cocteau Twins and Harold Budd, Steely Dan and Prefab Sprout, rapping over the results like he's just been co-signed by Drain Gang. 

It's not particularly easy to digest but it is intriguing, thrusting forth a sturdy snapshot of the almost comically maligned Dimes Square scene, a "post-ironic" subculture that sat at the intersection of art, podcasting and internet culture. Whether you can handle that depends on your trivia, your tolerance and your general level of interest, we reckon. If you're into Elias Rønnenfelt's last record, 'Your Day Will Come' should at least press a few of the right buttons.

items.body:
Dutch techno duo Artefakt invite KMRU to assist on their third 'Collaborations' volume, improvising with the Kenyan sound artist in the studio to capture the immediacy of their exchange.

'Collaborations III' follows last year's short, sharp EP with Mayaan Nidam and its predecessor, a record of deep techno variations made alongside Sardinian producer Claudio PRC. This one's the series' most generous set so far and started life in 2023 when the trio found themselves at Pulse, a wooden cabin-cum-studio in the Brandeburg forest. This is where most of the improvisations were initially formulated and in the second session, at Artefakt's Berlin studio, they dubbed the two solo piano tracks and finished the arrangements. It's charming material, as you might imagine, that deviates from Artefakt's prior material and KMRU's noisy recent gear. Made mostly of pillowy, synth-led drones and subtle environmental sounds, it's prime gear for sinking into your surroundings to.

items.body:
New Dream Machine 12" from Dutch producer Kennedy.

"Kennedy continues to sketch out imaginary worlds where thoughts and sensations are converted into sound via the power of machines. On this fifth instalment of Hi-Tech Soul, the Dutch producer channels fragments of midnight memories and daytime visions into something tactile yet elusive. As with previous chapters, the process remains shaped by surprise as hands and hardware entwine in a quiet, freeform dialogue.

The music itself drifts rather than drives, unfolding like shifting cloud forms that never quite settle. Loose, frayed house patterns hover in a state of flotation as basslines anchor just enough to stop everything dissolving completely. Each track has a sense of elevation where melodic synths filter through the mix like heavenly sunbeams breaking overhead. There's a constant progression to something that never comes, instead leaving you free to find your own meaning as textures blur into something soft, indistinct and gently euphoric.

A pure state of celestial suspension, 'Dream 5' is the newest offering in a series that takes you to a weightless world of infinite interpretations."

items.body:
In the 15+ years that have elapsed since 'Loop Finding Jazz Records' first shuffled out of his ambrosially dusty speakers, Jan Jelinek's most famous album has acquired an almost mythical status. Originally released via Pole's defunct Scape imprint, it now finds new life via Jelinek's own Faitiche label, for a new generation to marvel at one of the finest examples of loop-based electronic music typical of the early noughties.

Taking what reads like a pretty austere set of ingredients, Jelinek's technique revolves around a trio of elements which consist of second long cuts of 1960's-70's jazz recordings, the loop-finding modulation wheel (do your homework!) and the Moiré effect; albeit rendered in the acoustic as opposed to the image and spectral domains.

If all this sounds a bit academic, be assured that on record it is anything but; as crumbling edifices of mealy rhythms slowly pulse into life and swirl around your head like snow storms clashing with a dust devil. Taking sediments of fathom deep static then skimming the best stuff from the top, Jelinek opens through the dampened echoes of 'Moiré (piano & organ)' wherein a slow-motion thrum of spiraling clicks, rustles and analogue tones conspire to give the impression of recondite perspectives that extend well beyond the constituent elements.

Elsewhere, 'Rocky in the Video Age' instills a gratuitously optimistic blush to the aquatic micro-sound ebb, 'Moiré (Strings)' is a perfect companion to Basinski's disintegrating tape archive, whilst 'Them, Their' represents an aural crease so sleight you can only catch its distinctive gleam from the corner of your eye.

items.body:
Simon Shreeve (Mønic, CUB) sifts and tweaks nine personal highlights of his cult transition from D&B to dubstep circa the late ‘00s/early 2010s, all acutely advised to acolytes of Youngsta, SP:MC, Icicle, Raime, The Bug x Ghost Dubs, Mick Harris...

By the time Kryptic Minds switched from darkest D&B to dubstep in 2009, they were arguably late to the game, but heavily made their presence felt with a five year string of classics for Loefah’s Swamp81, Tectonic, and their own label, Osiris Music UK, now considered canon to the sound. ‘The Things They Left Behind’ now dusts off and refines nine crucial examples of how they brought D&B production values to the heel of its rogue sibling, dubstep, firmly living up to El-B’s original dream of fusing late ‘90s tech-step and darker UKG, but also augmented with careful measures of atmospheric trip hop sensuality that place it in the long shadow of UK gloom shrouding Burial and Pinch bits.

Basically it’s a director’s cut of 2011 album ‘Can’t Sleep’, all “reimagined, refined and 2026 remastered” to best tell his tale of that pivotal era. In passage from the pensive title tune to cinematic closer ‘1000 Lost Cities’, he tightens the screws and checks the brakes on a definitive redux, edging the rictus halfstep tension of ‘No More No Less’, and a spidery 2-step dissection ‘Alone’, along with the relatively sublime levity of ‘Fade to Nothing’, and what sounds like ‘Mezzanine’-era Massive Attack gone halfstep on ‘Myth’, thru to the digitally shivered delays of ‘Depth of Field’ and slicker retread of ‘A Glimpse of Hope’.

items.body:
Long considered a diggers holy grail, 'African Skies' is a harp-led weightless jazz masterpiece from early Arkestra member and Chicago legend Kelan Phil Cohran - crucial, life affirming gear that’s compulsory listening for disciples of Sun Ra, Alice Coltrane, Dorothy Ashby, Chicago Underground.

In 1993, decades after his work with Sun Ra and long after he'd carved out a revered solo niche for himself with 'On the Beach' and 'Spanish Suite', Cohran was tapped by Chicago's Adler Planetarium to score a program they called African Skies - designed to reach out to the city's Black neighbourhoods and present the next generation with inspiration and education. Cohran was an obvious choice; he’d been working with young Chicago talent for years, opening the short-lived Afro-Arts Theatre in 1967 and running various educational initiatives for his community, teaching Black history and mentoring fresh talent.

The project aimed to present footage collected from observatories in Africa with music, tasking Cohran with recording suitably cosmic material for the score. Gathering collaborators Oscar Brown III (on string bass, piccolo bass and flute), Aquilla Sadalla (on bass clarinet, guitar, flute and vocals), Josefe Marie Verna (on harp, trombone and flute) and his son Malik Cohran (on guitar, string bass and flute), he set out to put together a kaleidoscopic soundtrack inspired by decades of research into devotional music, African history and archeo-astronomy.  The result is undoubtedly Cohran’s most ethereal suite, lifted to the heavens by his virtuosic performances on harp, trumpet, congas, violin uke, guitar, flute and his "space harp" the frankinphone -  an amplified lamellophone that Cohran designed after studying African instruments like the kalimba. 

Opening with the incendiary harp-led 'Theme', Cohran immediately hits the album's most-loved cue, the 10-minute devotional tour de fource 'White Nile'. Leading with harp, Cohran picks out stars from the wide, open skyline with notes that seem to ricochet off brown's basslines, while Sadalla's voice soars like a comet, heralding brass and woodwind flourishes in the track's jubilant second half. The record's flipside might be even more uplifting. On 'Sahara', each musician follows Cohran's jerky frankinphone phrasing as the band draw tight spirals that Cohran responds to with pitchy fiddle vamps. On 'Kalahari', each member of the quintet plays flute instinctively, coaxing out animalistic resonances, while 'Kilimanjaro' sends us off on a mutable rhythmic showpiece that's guided by the space harp's rhythmelodic clangs and clacks, forming a sturdy backbone for Sadalla's wordless scats.

A stunning set - finally available again for high definition consumption.

items.body:
Gary Sullivan, host of WFMU's Bodega Pop, pools his Brooklyn and Queens finds on this crunchy anthology, collecting early 20th century Russian music that was prized by first-generation Russian New Yorkers.

Time's frozen on 'Let Me Perish Without Return', a set of noisy ballads, music hall standards and folky reflections that map out the experience of the diaspora who immigrated from the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union as the home they knew transformed beyond recognition. Sullivan combed thrift stores in Forest Hills, Brighton Beach and Gravesend to find these intriguing cues, and pieces together a story that's shared by half a million New Yorkers. The remnants of Russian life are still visible on the surface of these neighborhoods, and the music helps us understand the culture a little more deeply. It's not particularly familiar material, but it makes for fascinating listening - especially if you've rinsed the rest of the Death is Not the End catalog.

items.body:
After a few trips ‘Around the Sun’ Mr Fingers returns to the ‘floor with a definitively broad selection of deep house and acid aces betraying the sound’s links with soul jazz as much as Italo disco and ambient synth musics.

‘Leev Ur Mynd’ is the prescriptive title of Larry Heard’s 7th studio LP in his OG mode, which lands just over 40 years since his early 12”s initiated a sea-change in club music. On a dozen cuts the veteran effortlessly ushers debonaire dancefloors to his command, from proper ChItalo acid peacockery in ‘Plastic Nightmares’ to the piquant electro-soul flow of ‘Replicate’, and covering the finest spectrum of styles & patterns within a theme in between. 

His influential mastery of the 303 results in thee juiciest acid on the LP title tune, then tweaked to a charming type of bloozy jig in ‘Barndance’, and woven into the album’s tuffest jam ‘Menagerie’, or more subtly riding the piano-led glyde of ‘April Rain’, whereas the rest tends towards his equal bias for slicker soul-jazz and Afro-Latinate slink. Deeper lounge lizards will get theirs in the syncopated shimmy of ‘The Happening Thing’ and the sublime vocal chops of ‘When You Need Me’ and ‘All I Need’, thru the frankly sexy ‘Tension’ and that chef’s kiss twinkle of percussion and choral pads in ‘Ribbons.’

What a G?! Tip!

items.body:
Strut Records presents a new reissue of the original Afrobeat classic Low Profile (Not For The Blacks), recorded and composed by Afrika 70 saxophonist and bandleader Lekan Animashaun and produced by Fela Kuti.

"After years touring the world as Fela’s baritone saxophonist, Animashaun stepped forward to lead the legendary Egypt 80 band following Tony Allen’s departure, remaining the group’s musical director until Fela’s death in 1997. He continued on subsequent tours with Seun Kuti until 2016.

Lekan began recording his only solo project, Low Profile, in 1977. The album was composed and recorded across sessions at home in Nigeria and on tour with Fela, who both produced the recordings and added keyboards to the album’s title track. ‘Low Profile (Not For The Blacks)’ referenced a government campaign during the country’s 1970s oil boom: “It was inspired by a speech by Olusegun Obasanjo, Nigeria’s military Head of State, when he urged black people to keep a low profile about their wealth and not to behave in a vulgar, arrogant way,” explains Lekan. “I argued that low profile is not just for the blacks, as everyone is human, regardless of race.” On the flip side, the simmering Afrobeat anthem ‘Se Rere’ (which translates as ‘Do Right’) delivers Animashaun’s message of living with integrity: do right, and you will reap what you sow. The song later became the band’s opening number during Fela’s live performances both in Nigeria and internationally throughout the 1980s and ’90s.

Despite recording beginning almost two decades earlier, Low Profile did not receive an official release until 1995, when it finally surfaced on Fela’s Kalakuta label. One of only a handful of albums led by core members of Kuti’s band, Low Profile captures a pivotal moment in Afrobeat history. Over time, the original has become a rare and highly sought-after record, and this new reissue places the spotlight back on a modest but influential Nigerian legend."

items.body:
Bitchin' Bajas' Cooper Crain and Chicago mainstay Bill MacKay follow 2023's hazed 'Foreign Smokes' with another blunted blend of kosmische, West Coast new age, psychedelia and folk rock.

If you like Bitchin' Bajas, particularly their collaborations with Natural Information Society, there's a damn good chance that 'Stash' will hit you right in the third eye. We already know the Crain and MacKay are weathered players and we already know that their minds are in sync; 'Stash' picks up where its predecessor left off, providing a cinematic answer to the duo's obsession with classic American rock, German psych, vintage British folk, French exotica, Arab pop and Bollywood music. It's not subtle, but with just two basic instruments - Crain flips between organ and synth, while MacKay plays guitar - they don't have the need to pussyfoot. 'Stash' is never overworked, it's the result of two friends jamming out, plugging their instruments into a mixing desk and recording to 8-track to get the grit the material needs.
